The estimation of interaction and quadratic effects in regression models with observed variables is a well-known procedure [@aiken_west_1991; @rimpler_etall_2025]. In that case, an interaction is calculated by the product of certain predictors, whereas a quadratic term involves the product of a predictor with itself. This allows researchers to study, for example, the dependency that one variable may have on the level of another variable. In a structural equation model (SEM) we usually have a regression function with latent variables (i.e., latent variable model or structural part; @bollen_model_2019). The triviality of estimating interaction and quadratic effects in this setting goes away because the scores (i.e., the subject-specific values) on the latent variables are, at least at the time of measurement, unobserved [@bollen_latent_2012]. Thus, one is not able to construct product terms as in the setting of a regression among observed variables. 

Despite that, the possibility to estimate latent interaction and quadratic terms is important. Indeed, for example, previous research (with observed variables) suggests that quadratic and interaction effects may "mask" or distort each other when predictors are correlated, which may lead to incorrect conclusions about the nature and direction of effects if not estimated simultaneously [@belzak_interaction_2019; @ganzach_misleading_1997]. Second, researchers in social and behavioral sciences should not have their theoretical models constrained by technical limitations — if theory suggests nonlinear effects exist, appropriate methods should be available to test these hypotheses rigorously. Moreover, SEM explicitly models measurement error in these product terms by partitioning variance into latent constructs and error terms, where this depends on the validity of our measurement model assumptions. This is particularly important because the reliability of a product term is lower than that of its components [@ng_chan_2020]. Thus, estimating interactions with latent variables would provide us with predictors that, in theory, do not contain measurement error. This also has consequences with respect to minimizing bias in the estimates for the regression parameters in the structural model. Adding to that, Marsh et al. (2012, as cited in Cham et al., 2012) highlighted that a latent variable model contributes to higher statistical power, but this may not necessarily hold in general [@Fuller1987].

Hence, multiple methods have been proposed in recent years that reflect successive attempts to address specific limitations identified in previous methods [@kenny_judd_1984; @joreskog_yan_1996; @algina_moulder_2001; @klein_moosbrugger_2000; @marsh_etall_2004; @bollen_1995; @wall_amemiya_gapi_2001; @mooijaart_bentler_2010; @mooijaart_satorra_2012; @boker_etall_2023]. However, these approaches differ substantially in their practical accessibility and in the assumptions required for their estimators to maintain desirable properties. For a detailed theoretical overview of assumptions and expected performance, we refer the reader to @kelava_brandt_2022. Building on this, simulation studies [@marsh_etall_2004; @cham_etall_2012; @brandt_etall_2014; @brandt_etall_2020; @lonati_etall_2025] have provided empirical evaluations of these methods' performance, offering general guidelines and findings with respect to, for example, bias, type I error rate, power, and efficiency across the different approaches under different conditions. The connection between previous findings and the current results is explicitly made in the discussion. Importantly, given the extensive literature, in this manuscript we focus mainly on the approaches used in our simulation study^[There are many others which are not investigated in this article and therefore are just briefly described here. @bollen_1995 introduced the model-implied instrumental variables two-stage least-squares (MIIV-2SLS) approach. @mooijaart_bentler_2010 proposed a methods-of-moments (MM) approach. More recently, a Products of Variables Model (PoV) approach was developed @boker_etall_2023. There are also other nonparametric approaches and bayesian estimation approaches. In fact, the Nonlinear Structural Equation Mixture Model (NSEMM) is an extension for the LMS that also uses full-information estimation but relaxes normality assumptions by integrating semiparametric estimation approaches [@kelava_etall_2014]. This approach despite showing good performance under structural and distributional misspecifications [@brandt_etall_2020] is not widely used.].

The initial approach, the so-called Product Indicator (PI) approach [@kenny_judd_1984], was based on constructing product indicators of the nonlinear latent variables by multiplying the indicators of the latent variables included in the interaction or quadratic term. Importantly, early implementations imposed restrictive multiple nonlinear constraints [@joreskog_yan_1996; @kelava_etall_2011]. Subsequent developments relaxed these constraints: the Generalized Appended Product Indicators (GAPI) approach removed normality assumptions for predictor latent variables [@wall_amemiya_gapi_2001], while the Unconstrained Product Indicators (UPI) approach^[The Extended Unconstrained Approach (ExUC) further extended UPI to handle both quadratic and interaction effects [@kelava_brandt_2009].] eliminated parameter constraints entirely [@marsh_etall_2004]. Research has also explored optimal strategies for constructing product indicators and various centering approaches, including mean-centering, residual centering, and double mean centering [@marsh_etall_2004; @schoemann_jorgensen_2021; @kjell_etall_2024]. 

Another relevant class of approaches is the distribution analytic approaches. These approaches address the normality violations inherent in product indicator methods without creating measurement models for nonlinear terms [@klein_moosbrugger_2000; @kelava_nonlinear_2014]. The Latent Moderated Structural Equations (LMS) approach approximates non-normal distributions using mixtures of normal distributions, partitioning latent variables into subvectors for nonlinear and linear terms, then applying the EM algorithm to integrate the weighted multivariate distributions [@klein_moosbrugger_2000; @kelava_brandt_2022]. The Quasi-Maximum Likelihood (QML) approach offers a computationally efficient alternative in contrast to the LMS by replacing complex non-normal distributions with normal approximations that preserve the same mean and variance, creating normally distributed components that allow the use of standard maximum likelihood techniques with minimal efficiency loss. 

Although LMS and UPI have gained wider adoption for modeling latent interactions and quadratic terms—which should increase given the recent accessibility improvements through the R package modsem—both methods encounter scalability limitations as the number of higher-order terms increases. UPI becomes computationally impractical as more product indicators are needed, which inflates model matrices and creates convergence difficulties. Similarly, LMS requires numerical integration at each iteration, rapidly constraining feasibility to models containing relatively few latent variables. While QML reduces computational demands compared to LMS, performance still diminishes as nonlinear components increase. Moreover, these approaches may rely on distributional assumptions, which the specific requirements depend on the chosen estimator. The UPI is typically estimated using maximum likelihood (ML), where consistency targets the mean-covariance structure without requiring multivariate normality of observed indicators. Normality assumptions are invoked to justify the likelihood's sampling distribution—specifically, the chi-square test statistic and normal-theory standard errors. When indicators exhibit nonnormality (which is typical given that product terms are inherently nonnormal), standard errors and fit statistics become unreliable; robust corrections (sandwich/Satorra-Bentler estimators) may provide asymptotic improvements but can remain underestimated in small samples. Furthermore, simulation studies indicate minimal improvement from these corrections [@cham_etall_2021; @lonati_etall_2024]. Conversely, LMS incorporates normality assumptions for latent predictors, measurement errors, and structural disturbances through the integrated likelihood; when these assumptions are satisfied, LMS provides ML-consistent and efficient estimates, though violations can introduce moderate bias and preclude the use of conventional global fit indices. QML makes similar normality assumptions to LMS but uses a quasi-likelihood approximation that replaces the nonnormal conditional distribution with a normal distribution having equivalent first and second moments, which may provide greater robustness to assumption violations at the cost of some efficiency. 

@rosseel_etall_2025 recently proposed a novel approach that addresses some of those limitations: the *local structural-after-measurement approach (LSAM)*^[In fact, this approach is closely connected to the more general two-stage method of moments (2SMM) [@wall_amemiya_2000; @wall_amemiya_2003]. As noted in @rosseel_etall_2025, and opposed to the 2SMM, the LSAM does not require the structural part to be recursive, nor needs to distinguish in advance between endogenous and exogenous variables. Moreover, it is not needed to center the latent predictors involved in the nonlinear effects. Importantly, both do not require the latent predictors to follow a normal distribution.]. In the original article, a small simulation study was conducted to evaluate the LSAM approach. The primary scope was limited, however, to examining the bias and variability of the point estimates involved in the interaction and quadratic terms. Therefore, the aim of this paper is to further extend it by analyzing standard errors^[Initially, one could only bootstrap to obtain standard errors in the LSAM, but it is now possible to obtain analytical two-step SEs. Future work will elaborate on this showing the connections with the 2SMM], coverage, type I error rate, and power. To study the performance of the LSAM, we will compare it with some of the more widely used and available methods in one simulation study: LMS, UPI with double-mean centering (DBLCENT), and QML approach. This simulation study will investigate standard errors, bias, coverage, type I error rate, and power. In a second simulation study will assess the "scalibility" of the LSAM approach. 

This paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we provide a brief overview of the statistical models under evaluation approaches, together with the distributional assumptions and its connections to the possible performance. We then present the simulation design, computational details, and performance measures. Following that, we report the results of our simulation studies. The last section concludes with a discussion that integrates our findings with the results from previous simulation studies.
